newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU pressure on Boeing heats up, no word on pacts.
newsitem.headline: EU pressure on Boeing heats up, no word on pacts.

text.p: Boeing's European office declined to comment on Wednesday on a newspaper report saying that the U.S. aircraft manufacturer is considering scrapping controversial supply pacts so that it can win EU approval for its merger with McDonnell Douglas.
"I have not heard that and I'm certainly in no position to comment", Boeing's communications director for Europe Craig Martin said.
But speculation was likely to build up in the coming weeks as both the antitrust authorities in the United States and in the European Union near a final decision on the $14 billion merger, he said.

"Clearly (European Competition Commissioner Karel) Van Miert has said he expects us to come back with some suggestions to meet his objections and I assume in some point Boeing will do, but I don't think we will be talking (to the press) about any specific suggestions that we may have," Craig said.

Van Miert has said he would not accept long-term exclusive supply agreements signed between Boeing and major U.S. airlines because they would shut out the airlines -- AMR's American Airlines and Delta Air Lines and more recently Continental Airlines -- from other aircraft makers.
Boeing's archrival Airbus Industrie said last week that the merger was ultimately aimed at eliminating it.
The Commission must take a final decision on the Boeing merger by July 31 at the latest. It is tentatively putting the issue on the agenda for July 23.

But a committee of antitrust experts from the EU's 15 states will meet already on July 4 on a draft proposal. Van Miert warned last week that the two partners should have no doubt about the Commission's determination to block the merger if no concessions were made.

The Wall Street Journal said on Wednesday, citing unnamed sources, that Boeing was considering scrapping the exclusivity provision in its agreements with the three airlines. But it would leave firm orders placed intact.

That the supply pacts will have to go is no surprise. But Commission officials have also clearly said that that alone did not solve the competition problems posed by the fact that the merger reduces the number of players in the commercial aviation sector from three to a mere two -- Boeing and Airbus.
Airbus is consortium owned by France's Aerospatiale, Daimler-Benz's Aerospace, British Aerospace and Construcciones Aeronauticas from Spain. -- Amelia Torres 322 2876841
